raw_evidence.content: The single biggest interpretive hook for this dataset. AI is now the gravitational center of arXiv's growth.

raw_evidence.label: arXiv: born 1991 as a physics email server
raw_evidence.content: arXiv began on August 14, 1991, when physicist Paul Ginsparg, newly arrived at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) in New Mexico, set up an automated email/FTP server (originally xxx.lanl.gov) so high-energy theoretical physicists could circulate preprints without waiting on slow journal review. Ginsparg built the prototype with simple csh scripts on his NeXT machine and expected maybe 100 submissions a year from a small community; it took 400 in its first six months. The server moved with Ginsparg to Cornell University in 2001, where it is operated today by Cornell Tech and the Cornell University Library. The four CSV files in this dataset are the public-facing statistics of that same system, three decades on. This origin matters for reading the data: the monthly submissions series (get_monthly_submissions.csv) literally starts in 1991-07 with a count of 2 papers, capturing the entire lifespan of the platform.

raw_evidence.label: The AI boom: why CS categories exploded post-2022
raw_evidence.content: The single biggest interpretive hook for this dataset. The Transformer architecture was introduced in the June 2017 arXiv preprint 'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv:1706.03762) — itself posted to arXiv before NeurIPS 2017. That architecture became the backbone of large language models, and ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022 detonated a research gold rush. In arXiv's stats this shows up as explosive growth in computer-science categories — cs.LG (Machine Learning), cs.CV (Computer Vision), and cs.CL (Computation and Language, i.e. NLP/LLMs) — which together accounted for over 6,000 new submissions in a single month (October 2024). cs.AI rides the same wave. So when the analyst finds the grp_cs categories (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CV) bending sharply upward across 2022-2025 in submissions_by_category.csv, the cause is the transformer/LLM/ChatGPT era. AI is now the gravitational center of arXiv's growth.

raw_evidence.content: arXiv began on August 14, 1991, when physicist Paul Ginsparg, newly arrived at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) in New Mexico, set up an automated email/FTP server (originally xxx.lanl.gov) so high-energy theoretical physicists could circulate preprints without waiting on slow journal review. Ginsparg built the prototype with simple csh scripts on his NeXT machine and expected maybe 100 submissions a year from a small community; it took 400 in its first six months. The server moved with Ginsparg to Cornell University in 2001, where it is operated today by Cornell Tech and the Cornell University Library. The four CSV files in this dataset are the public-facing statistics of that same system, three decades on. This origin matters for reading the data: the monthly submissions series (get_monthly_submissions.csv) literally starts in 1991-07 with a count of 2 papers, capturing the entire lifespan of the platform.

By letting anyone read the latest work for free, immediately, it became one of the precipitating forces behind the open-access movement in scholarly publishing. Ginsparg won a MacArthur 'genius' Fellowship in 2002 and the Einstein Foundation Berlin Award in 2021 for creating it. The platform runs on a modest budget (about $826,000/year in the 2013-2017 era) funded by Cornell, the Simons Foundation, and member-institution fees of roughly $1,000-$4,400/year — a striking contrast to the multi-billion-dollar commercial journal industry it disrupts. In March 2026 arXiv announced it will become an independent nonprofit on July 1, 2026. For a general reader, the stakes are: this is the infrastructure on which modern physics, math, and AI research is actually shared.

raw_evidence.label: From 2 papers/month to 3 million: the 1991-2025 arc
raw_evidence.content: arXiv's full-history submission series captures the entire lifespan of the platform, from 2 papers in its first month (July 1991) to a mature output of roughly 24,000-27,000 papers per month in 2024-2025. Annual submissions climbed almost monotonically every single year: 306 in the partial 1991, 3,263 in the first full year (1992), 30,601 by 2000, 70,131 by 2010, 178,329 by 2020, and 284,486 in 2025. Cumulatively, arXiv crossed 500,000 papers in October 2008, 1 million in December 2014, 2 million in January 2022, and 2.5 million in June 2024; the running total stands at about 3.05 million through 2026-05. These crossings line up almost exactly with the externally documented milestones in det_04, confirming the series is the real arXiv corpus.

yr = hist.groupby('year')['submissions'].sum()
print("Annual submission totals (full history):")
for y, v in yr.items():
    print(f"  {y}: {int(v)}")
print(f"First month 1991-07: {int(hist[hist['month']=='1991-07']['submissions'].iloc[0])}")
print(f"2024 total: {int(yr.get(2024,0))}")
# milestone crossings (cumulative)
hist_sorted = hist.sort_values('dt').copy()
hist_sorted['cum'] = hist_sorted['submissions'].cumsum()

raw_evidence.label: From 2 papers/month to 3 million: the 1991-2025 arc
raw_evidence.content: arXiv's full-history submission series captures the entire lifespan of the platform, from 2 papers in its first month (July 1991) to a mature output of roughly 24,000-27,000 papers per month in 2024-2025. Annual submissions climbed almost monotonically every single year: 306 in the partial 1991, 3,263 in the first full year (1992), 30,601 by 2000, 70,131 by 2010, 178,329 by 2020, and 284,486 in 2025. Cumulatively, arXiv crossed 500,000 papers in October 2008, 1 million in December 2014, 2 million in January 2022, and 2.5 million in June 2024; the running total stands at about 3.05 million through 2026-05. These crossings line up almost exactly with the externally documented milestones in det_04, confirming the series is the real arXiv corpus.
raw_evidence.code:
yr = hist.groupby('year')['submissions'].sum()
print("Annual submission totals (full history):")
for y, v in yr.items():
    print(f"  {y}: {int(v)}")
print(f"First month 1991-07: {int(hist[hist['month']=='1991-07']['submissions'].iloc[0])}")
print(f"2024 total: {int(yr.get(2024,0))}")
# milestone crossings (cumulative)
hist_sorted = hist.sort_values('dt').copy()
hist_sorted['cum'] = hist_sorted['submissions'].cumsum()
for milestone in [500_000, 1_000_000, 2_000_000, 2_500_000]:
    cross = hist_sorted[hist_sorted['cum'] >= milestone]
    if len(cross):
        r = cross.iloc[0]
        print(f"  cumulative {milestone:,} crossed at {r['month']} (cum={int(r['cum']):,})")
print(f"Total cumulative submissions through {hist_sorted['month'].iloc[-1]}: {int(hist_sorted['cum'].iloc[-1]):,}")

# --- ana_02: CAGR of monthly submission rate ---
print("=== ana_02 ===")
# use complete calendar years only for CAGR (1992 first full year, 2025 last full year)
full_yr = yr[(yr.index >= 1992) & (yr.index <= 2025)]
start_y, end_y = 1992, 2025
v0, v1 = full_yr[start_y], full_yr[end_y]
n = end_y - start_y
cagr = (v1/v0)**(1/n) - 1

raw_evidence.label: The AI boom: why CS categories exploded post-2022
raw_evidence.content: The single biggest interpretive hook for this dataset. The Transformer architecture was introduced in the June 2017 arXiv preprint 'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv:1706.03762) — itself posted to arXiv before NeurIPS 2017. That architecture became the backbone of large language models, and ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022 detonated a research gold rush. In arXiv's stats this shows up as explosive growth in computer-science categories — cs.LG (Machine Learning), cs.CV (Computer Vision), and cs.CL (Computation and Language, i.e. NLP/LLMs) — which together accounted for over 6,000 new submissions in a single month (October 2024). cs.AI rides the same wave. So when the analyst finds the grp_cs categories (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CV) bending sharply upward across 2022-2025 in submissions_by_category.csv, the cause is the transformer/LLM/ChatGPT era. AI is now the gravitational center of arXiv's growth.

raw_evidence.label: AI-first publishing culture: arXiv as the field's town square
raw_evidence.content: Machine-learning research developed a distinctive 'arXiv-first' culture: results are posted to arXiv the moment they're ready — often before, or instead of, formal conference/journal publication — because the field moves too fast for traditional timelines. Citing an arXiv preprint is normal practice in CS in a way it never was in, say, biology. The 'Attention Is All You Need' title even spawned a self-replicating meme: at least 717 arXiv preprints from 2009-2025 carry 'All You Need' in their title, growing exponentially after 2017. This culture amplifies the submission counts: arXiv is not a sidecar to CS/AI publishing, it IS the primary venue of record for much of the field, which is part of why CS submissions dwarf other groups in the recent data.

Those three together accounted for over 6,000 new submissions in October 2024

raw_evidence.label: AI-first publishing culture: arXiv as the field's town square
raw_evidence.content: Machine-learning research developed a distinctive 'arXiv-first' culture: results are posted to arXiv the moment they're ready — often before, or instead of, formal conference/journal publication — because the field moves too fast for traditional timelines. Citing an arXiv preprint is normal practice in CS in a way it never was in, say, biology. The 'Attention Is All You Need' title even spawned a self-replicating meme: at least 717 arXiv preprints from 2009-2025 carry 'All You Need' in their title, growing exponentially after 2017. This culture amplifies the submission counts: arXiv is not a sidecar to CS/AI publishing, it IS the primary venue of record for much of the field, which is part of why CS submissions dwarf other groups in the recent data.

sources.title: 'All You Need' is Not All You Need for a Paper Title: On the Origins of a Scientific Meme
facts: 717 arXiv preprints contained 'All You Need' in their titles from 2009-2025
These show exponential growth following the original 2017 paper

raw_evidence.label: cs.LG is the single biggest category on arXiv
raw_evidence.content: Across the 2022-01 to 2025-09 window (1.57 million submissions over 155 categories), the four AI categories own the top of the table: cs.LG (Machine Learning) is #1 with 134,903 submissions (8.6% of everything), followed by cs.AI (101,916, 6.5%), cs.CV (Computer Vision, 100,238, 6.4%) and cs.CL (NLP/LLMs, 61,144, 3.9%). The first non-CS category is quant-ph at #5 (47,902, 3.0%), less than half of cs.CV. The long tail is steep: the smallest categories have only a few hundred submissions (cs.GL has just 56). This ranking is the structural fingerprint of the transformer/LLM era described in det_05.
raw_evidence.code:
for c, v in tot.head(20).items():
    print(f"  {c}: {int(v):,} ({v/grand*100:.1f}%)")
print("Bottom 10 categories:")
for c, v in tot.tail(10).items():
    print(f"  {c}: {int(v):,}")

# --- ana_11: Concentration - top 10 share ---
print("=== ana_11 ===")
top10share = tot.head(10).sum()/grand*100
top4share = tot.head(4).sum()/grand*100
print(f"Top 10 of 155 categories account for {top10share:.1f}% of all submissions")
print(f"Top 4 (cs.LG/CV/CL/AI?) account for {top4share:.1f}%")
cumshare = (tot.cumsum()/grand*100)
for k in [1,3,5,10,20,50]:
    print(f"  top {k}: {cumshare.iloc[k-1]:.1f}% cumulative")
print(f"Top 4 categories: {list(tot.head(4).index)}")

raw_evidence.editorial_notes: Top-4 = 25.3%; cs.LG = 134,903 (largest single category). Optional image det_media_03 (Geoffrey Hinton) to put a face on the AI boom — Designer's call. Do NOT sum mirrored category pairs in the ranking chart (ana_23).

raw_evidence.label: The AI boom: why CS categories exploded post-2022
raw_evidence.content: The single biggest interpretive hook for this dataset. The Transformer architecture was introduced in the June 2017 arXiv preprint 'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv:1706.03762) — itself posted to arXiv before NeurIPS 2017. That architecture became the backbone of large language models, and ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022 detonated a research gold rush. In arXiv's stats this shows up as explosive growth in computer-science categories — cs.LG (Machine Learning), cs.CV (Computer Vision), and cs.CL (Computation and Language, i.e. NLP/LLMs) — which together accounted for over 6,000 new submissions in a single month (October 2024). cs.AI rides the same wave. So when the analyst finds the grp_cs categories (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CV) bending sharply upward across 2022-2025 in submissions_by_category.csv, the cause is the transformer/LLM/ChatGPT era. AI is now the gravitational center of arXiv's growth.

Those three together accounted for over 6,000 new submissions in October 2024

raw_evidence.label: AI-first publishing culture: arXiv as the field's town square
raw_evidence.content: Machine-learning research developed a distinctive 'arXiv-first' culture: results are posted to arXiv the moment they're ready — often before, or instead of, formal conference/journal publication — because the field moves too fast for traditional timelines. Citing an arXiv preprint is normal practice in CS in a way it never was in, say, biology. The 'Attention Is All You Need' title even spawned a self-replicating meme: at least 717 arXiv preprints from 2009-2025 carry 'All You Need' in their title, growing exponentially after 2017. This culture amplifies the submission counts: arXiv is not a sidecar to CS/AI publishing, it IS the primary venue of record for much of the field, which is part of why CS submissions dwarf other groups in the recent data.

sources.title: 'All You Need' is Not All You Need for a Paper Title: On the Origins of a Scientific Meme
facts: 717 arXiv preprints contained 'All You Need' in their titles from 2009-2025
These show exponential growth following the original 2017 paper

raw_evidence.label: cs.LG is the single biggest category on arXiv
raw_evidence.content: Across the 2022-01 to 2025-09 window (1.57 million submissions over 155 categories), the four AI categories own the top of the table: cs.LG (Machine Learning) is #1 with 134,903 submissions (8.6% of everything), followed by cs.AI (101,916, 6.5%), cs.CV (Computer Vision, 100,238, 6.4%) and cs.CL (NLP/LLMs, 61,144, 3.9%). The first non-CS category is quant-ph at #5 (47,902, 3.0%), less than half of cs.CV. The long tail is steep: the smallest categories have only a few hundred submissions (cs.GL has just 56). This ranking is the structural fingerprint of the transformer/LLM era described in det_05.
raw_evidence.code:
for c, v in tot.head(20).items():
    print(f"  {c}: {int(v):,} ({v/grand*100:.1f}%)")
print("Bottom 10 categories:")
for c, v in tot.tail(10).items():
    print(f"  {c}: {int(v):,}")

# --- ana_11: Concentration - top 10 share ---
print("=== ana_11 ===")
top10share = tot.head(10).sum()/grand*100
top4share = tot.head(4).sum()/grand*100
print(f"Top 10 of 155 categories account for {top10share:.1f}% of all submissions")
print(f"Top 4 (cs.LG/CV/CL/AI?) account for {top4share:.1f}%")
cumshare = (tot.cumsum()/grand*100)
for k in [1,3,5,10,20,50]:
    print(f"  top {k}: {cumshare.iloc[k-1]:.1f}% cumulative")
print(f"Top 4 categories: {list(tot.head(4).index)}")

raw_evidence.label: The AI boom: why CS categories exploded post-2022
raw_evidence.content: The single biggest interpretive hook for this dataset. The Transformer architecture was introduced in the June 2017 arXiv preprint 'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv:1706.03762) — itself posted to arXiv before NeurIPS 2017. That architecture became the backbone of large language models, and ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022 detonated a research gold rush. In arXiv's stats this shows up as explosive growth in computer-science categories — cs.LG (Machine Learning), cs.CV (Computer Vision), and cs.CL (Computation and Language, i.e. NLP/LLMs) — which together accounted for over 6,000 new submissions in a single month (October 2024). cs.AI rides the same wave. So when the analyst finds the grp_cs categories (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CV) bending sharply upward across 2022-2025 in submissions_by_category.csv, the cause is the transformer/LLM/ChatGPT era. AI is now the gravitational center of arXiv's growth.

raw_evidence.label: Group composition shift: CS to ~47% of arXiv
raw_evidence.content: At the group level, computer science has pulled away from physics as arXiv's largest field. Comparing the first 12 months (2022) to the trailing 12 months (2024-10..2025-09): CS rose from 36.7% to 46.7% of all submissions (+9.9 percentage points, growing 1.85x in volume), while physics fell from 34.9% to 28.9% (-6.0pp) and math from 17.7% to 14.6% (-3.2pp) despite both still growing ~20% in absolute terms. Every non-CS group lost share simply because CS grew so much faster. The smaller groups (econ, q-fin, q-bio) grew a respectable ~50-60% but from tiny bases (each well under 1% of total). The story is not that other fields shrank — it's that CS ate the growth.

raw_evidence.label: Why arXiv matters: open science & access
raw_evidence.content: arXiv's significance is that it democratized access to cutting-edge research. By letting anyone read the latest work for free, immediately, it became one of the precipitating forces behind the open-access movement in scholarly publishing. Ginsparg won a MacArthur 'genius' Fellowship in 2002 and the Einstein Foundation Berlin Award in 2021 for creating it. The platform runs on a modest budget (about $826,000/year in the 2013-2017 era) funded by Cornell, the Simons Foundation, and member-institution fees of roughly $1,000-$4,400/year — a striking contrast to the multi-billion-dollar commercial journal industry it disrupts. In March 2026 arXiv announced it will become an independent nonprofit on July 1, 2026. For a general reader, the stakes are: this is the infrastructure on which modern physics, math, and AI research is actually shared.

raw_evidence.label: Readership scaled to ~410M downloads/year
raw_evidence.content: Demand grew alongside supply. Annual full-text downloads rose from 128,204 in 1994 to 9.1 million in 2000, 39.9 million in 2010, 136.3 million in 2015, 334.6 million in 2020, and 410.1 million in 2025 — a roughly 3,000-fold increase over three decades. Recent monthly downloads average about 34 million, and the single busiest month on record is November 2023 with 54.75 million. IMPORTANT DATA-QUALITY CAVEAT: the downloads file has a 13-month gap — it jumps straight from 2023-11 to 2025-01, so all of December 2023 and the entire 2024 calendar year are missing. Any annual download chart must either show the gap or omit 2024 rather than imply a collapse.
raw_evidence.code:
dyr = dls.groupby('year')['downloads'].sum()
# years with full 12 months only, for annual totals
ymon = dls.groupby('year')['month'].nunique()
print("Annual downloads (selected COMPLETE years):")
for y in [1994, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023, 2025]:
    if y in dyr.index:
        print(f"  {y}: {int(dyr[y]):,} ({ymon[y]} months)")
print(f"First nonzero month: {dls[dls['downloads']>0].iloc[0]['month']} = {int(dls[dls['downloads']>0].iloc[0]['downloads'])}")
# recent monthly download scale (2025, complete)
recent_dl = dls[(dls['dt']>='2025-01-01')&(dls['dt']<'2026-01-01')][['month','downloads']]
print(f"Mean monthly downloads 2025: {recent_dl['downloads'].mean():,.0f}")
print(f"Peak month: {dls.loc[dls['downloads'].idxmax(),'month']} = {int(dls['downloads'].max()):,}")

# --- ana_06: Downloads-vs-submissions relationship ---
print("=== ana_06 ===")
# align on month over overlapping range
mh = hist[['month','submissions']].copy()
md = dls[['month','downloads']].copy()
merged = mh.merge(md, on='month', how='inner')
merged['dt'] = pd.to_datetime(merged['month'])
# downloads per submission ratio over time
merged['dl_per_sub'] = merged['downloads'] / merged['submissions']

raw_evidence.content: Monthly submissions and monthly downloads are tightly correlated across the 375 overlapping months: Pearson r = 0.936 (log-log r = 0.943). But downloads have grown faster than submissions, so reads-per-submission climbed steadily — from about 299 downloads per new paper in 2000, to 569 in 2010, to 1,889 in 2020. In other words, each new paper now commands far more attention than papers did two decades ago, reflecting both a larger global readership and the compounding value of the back-catalogue (old papers keep being downloaded). Supply and demand scale together, but demand scales harder.

raw_evidence.content: arXiv's significance is that it democratized access to cutting-edge research. By letting anyone read the latest work for free, immediately, it became one of the precipitating forces behind the open-access movement in scholarly publishing. Ginsparg won a MacArthur 'genius' Fellowship in 2002 and the Einstein Foundation Berlin Award in 2021 for creating it. The platform runs on a modest budget (about $826,000/year in the 2013-2017 era) funded by Cornell, the Simons Foundation, and member-institution fees of roughly $1,000-$4,400/year — a striking contrast to the multi-billion-dollar commercial journal industry it disrupts. In March 2026 arXiv announced it will become an independent nonprofit on July 1, 2026. For a general reader, the stakes are: this is the infrastructure on which modern physics, math, and AI research is actually shared.

raw_evidence.label: The AI-slop crisis & 2025 moderation crackdown
raw_evidence.content: A controversy directly relevant to the tail end of this dataset (which runs to 2025-10). Despite fears after ChatGPT, arXiv saw no spike in problematic submissions through 2024 — but in early 2025 'AI slop' (LLM-generated filler papers, especially review/survey articles) rose exponentially, starting in computer science and spreading. Moderator rejection rates climbed from the historical ~4% to about 10-12%. arXiv now receives 'hundreds of review articles every month.' In October 2025, arXiv announced it would no longer accept review or position papers in computer science unless they had already passed journal/conference peer review. This is a crucial caveat: any flattening, dip, or composition shift in cs.* categories in the final months of submissions_by_category.csv could reflect this October-2025 policy change, not a genuine decline in research. (Note also: the very last month in each per-category file, 2025-10, shows tiny counts like 13-76 — almost certainly a partial/incomplete data month, NOT a crash. The analyst should treat 2025-10 as truncated.)

raw_evidence.label: 2026 endorsement overhaul: an institutional email is no longer enough
raw_evidence.content: On January 21, 2026, arXiv changed who is allowed to submit. An institutional email address — for years the de facto key to the archive — is no longer sufficient to endorse a first-time submitter to a category. New authors must now either pair an institutional email with prior authorship on a paper already accepted in that endorsement domain, or obtain a personal endorsement from an established arXiv author in the field. arXiv said the change was forced by "an unsustainable increase in the number of non-scientific submissions, increasing the rejection rate and requiring excessive moderation and staff effort." Authors already endorsed in a category keep their status, and staff explicitly cannot waive the requirement. The same tightening was piloted on the Mathematics section in December 2025 before rolling out across all categories.

raw_evidence.content: A controversy directly relevant to the tail end of this dataset (which runs to 2025-10). Despite fears after ChatGPT, arXiv saw no spike in problematic submissions through 2024 — but in early 2025 'AI slop' (LLM-generated filler papers, especially review/survey articles) rose exponentially, starting in computer science and spreading. raw_evidence.label: 2026 endorsement overhaul: an institutional email is no longer enough
raw_evidence.content: On January 21, 2026, arXiv changed who is allowed to submit. An institutional email address — for years the de facto key to the archive — is no longer sufficient to endorse a first-time submitter to a category. New authors must now either pair an institutional email with prior authorship on a paper already accepted in that endorsement domain, or obtain a personal endorsement from an established arXiv author in the field. arXiv said the change was forced by "an unsustainable increase in the number of non-scientific submissions, increasing the rejection rate and requiring excessive moderation and staff effort." Authors already endorsed in a category keep their status, and staff explicitly cannot waive the requirement. The same tightening was piloted on the Mathematics section in December 2025 before rolling out across all categories.
